Lomi asked casually.

The goblin pilot didn't even turn his head. Reaching over with a clawed thumb, he hammered a red locking lever that set the mechanical legs on a fixed, dead-straight trajectory.

"A lot harder when you don't have idiots asking questions," the goblin grunted flatly.

"Buzz off.".

"Fair enough," Lomi chuckled, leaning against the navigation console.

"I'm Lomi. Just a harbor mechanic taking in the view. Really beautiful work on these suspension gyros, by the way.".

Lomi continuing to chat despite the tone of the driver, continued, "First time out of Vumbua, so I just thought I'd come up and take in the surroundings. It's beautiful out here.".

The goblin rolled his eyes, turning back to his dials.

"Buzz off, man.".

Unbothered by the feisty driver, Lomi looked out over the open savanna. Ahead in the tall grass, a narrow, razor-sharp wake parted the green blades like a miniature bow wave—an arrow of disturbance knifing straight across the plains. Every few seconds, the dark, glistening ridge of a massive shell surfaced before submerging beneath the grass.

Intrigued, Lomi studied the glowing acoustic holographic map projecting above the dashboard. The primary heading was plotted in crisp gold light across flat terrain. Looking back outside and comparing to the gauge Lomi noticed that the line the tortoise was cutting through the tall grass was running a degree or two off the walker's path. As he watched the tortoise quickly redirected, matching the heading of the Elijah, before twitching and snapping back it's off-axis trajectory like a beating heart signalling for attention. As it did, the map briefly showed a blip as if warning of a collission, before vanishing.

Lomi tapped the display console, nudging the goblin pilot.

"Hey... do you see what the turtle is doing on that acoustic track?".

The goblin squinted over the high brass dashboard, grimacing.

"I can't see over the damn dash, and I don't care to try. I follow the gold arrow. That's my job.".

Lomi turned to Professor Ink, who was watching him with keen, analytical curiosity.

"Professor," Lomi said, pointing to the shimmering teal trace.

"Is that stutter on the projection a navigational glitch? Watch it for a second.".

Professor Ink leaned over the console, her dark eyes narrowing.

"That is not a projection anomaly. That trace is tracking the acoustic resonance of the creature moving through the savanna."

She paused, her breath catching as she stared at the glass.

"Wait... what did you just say about a turtle?".

"The magic turtle," Lomi replied calmly.

Professor Ink went utterly rigid.

"I have heard about this turtle twice now....Interesting..."

Ink murmured, her eyes darting back to the plains. She gestured excitedly toward the parting grass.

"Tell me what you are seeing! This line here in the grass... it's a turtle running at... well it is an absurdly fast turtle".

" I mean, it's a magic turtle," Lomi chuckled, leaning against the brass rail. " So it's probably pretty quivck. Keep looking at it, Professor. Keep your eyes locked on the wake in the grass.".

"It is off by two degrees," Ink noted sharply, her analytical mind seizing on the discrepancy.

"Why?".

"That's the question," Lomi smiled.

"And it's about to snap in front of us. Just wait.".

Ahead in the grass, the green wake twitched and snapped abruptly back match the Elijah's vector - with the small map showing it's dot, before adjusting to it's original heading again, diverging from the Elijah.

Ink gasped softly.

"What was that? Why did it do that? Did you tell it to do that?".

"No, I didn't," Lomi answered, shaking his head.

"I just wanted to make sure you were seeing what I was seeing".

"That vector is to a different part of the forest," Ink murmured in rising wonder.

"That is to the center. That is not where the clans live.".

"I think we need to adjust our heading," Lomi said firmly.

"A big ask from a harbor mechanic," Ink challenged, raising an eyebrow.

Lomi flashed a confident grin.

"Hey... let me ask you something, Professor. Are you feeling lucky?".

Professor Ink, looked a Lomi for a moment before decisively turning to the helm.

"Adjust heading. Two degrees south-southwest.".

The goblin pilot turned around in his chair, glaring in complete disbelief.

"Are you seriously going to listen to this guy?!"

the goblin shouted.

"He just walked up here and started talking about a magic turtle running through the grass!".

"Set two degrees," Professor Ink commanded crisply.

"Lock the heading.".

The goblin grumbled, spinning the primary brass rudder until the walker's mechanical gait swung two degrees to port, aligning perfectly with the tortoise's wake.

Professor Ink pulled a small leather notepad from her vest, furiously scribbling notes.

"Lomi... I am about to look away from the savanna. Give me forty seconds, then ask me why we altered course.".

"Should I act angry?"

Lomi asked with a grin.

"Like you made a mistake?".

"No," Ink said seriously.

"Just instruct me to read my notes.".

She turned her back to the panoramic windows, staring fixedly at the blank mahogany bulkhead. Thirty seconds passed in dead silence. Forty seconds. Ink blinked, shook her head slightly, and turned back to Lomi with a polite, puzzled smile.

"Ah, Lomi. You were asking about our destination coordinates?".

"Doc," Lomi said without missing a beat, "we just drifted off the primary course. What are you doing?".

Professor Ink frowned in sudden alarm, looking at the helm.

"I didn't alter the course... you told me to alter course by two degrees! But why did I—" She stopped, her voice faltering as she stared into the terrifying blank space in her own memory.

"Check your notepad, Professor," Lomi told her gently.

"Make sure you didn't mess something up.".

Ink flipped open the notebook, reading her own frantic handwriting: Don't look at turtle. Cadets can see turtle. Follow turtle.

She let out a long, shuddering breath, closing the book.

"Lomi... how many people aboard this vessel can maintain continuous visual tracking on that creature?".

"At least seven of us," Lomi answered.

"Then we institute a permanent watch rotation," Professor Ink ordered.

"There must be one cadet stationed on this bridge at all times, keeping their eyes locked on the grass so the heading never drifts."

She moved toward the ladder hatch.

"I must confer with the research lab immediately.".

Chapter 12: The Forgetfulness & The Clans

CHAPTER 12: THE FORGETFULNESS & THE CLANS.

Professor Ink dropped down the ladder into the lower laboratory barge, her mind racing faster than her feet could move.

"Did Britt receive the stabilizer?"

Ink asked immediately, scanning the room.

"Is she cured?".

"Not cured," Rill answered from the counter.

"The progression has been delayed.".

"Delayed is good," Professor Ink breathed, steadying herself. She turned to the squad, her eyes shining with manic scientific excitement.

"We have established an unprecedented cognitive phenomenon. Every person in this room can see the Spirit Tortoise—what no one outside our party can do is retain the memory of having seen it! Out in the savanna, the moment your gaze leaves the creature, the entity completely erases its existence from your mind!".

Ignatius stepped into the center of the lab, holding up both hands.

"Hold on, hold on. Are you saying we're the only ones in the entire empire who can actually see the damn turtle?!".

"Not the only ones who can see it," Ink clarified.

"Anyone can see it when looking directly at it. The trick is that breaking visual contact erases the memory from the observer's mind.".

"It makes people forget," Britt whispered, her eyes wide as the ancient lore pieces aligned.

Ignatius looked around the room.

"Raise your hand if you remember the turtle right now.".

Every hand in the room went up—except Rill's, who wavered awkwardly.

"I remember talking about turtles... sort of," Rill muttered, her brow furrowing in frustration.

"Like a dream slipping away.".

Professor Ink held up her leather notepad.

"I had originally planned to navigate Elijah straight to the Mizizi clan to consult your clan elders regarding the node synchronization failure. But every instinct demands we follow this tortoise instead. Britt... what does your clan lore say about these entities?".

"Our people live alongside the tortoises," Britt explained softly, coming to a decision in her mind to finally trust Professor Ink and the scholars, realizing that there was something that needed to be solved here, "The tradition has always been to maintain careful distance and never interfere with their path. But this creature approached us. It sought us out.".

"Is there a formal law governing interaction?"

Ink pressed.

"Not a written law," Britt said.

"A social norm passed down through generations: leave them be. Do not look at them, do not touch them, and never follow them.".

"And you looked at it," Professor Ink observed sharply.

"And Rill said you touched it last night in the forest. And what happened?".

"Pip was pulled inside its memory space," Britt revealed, glancing at Aggie.

"And when we touched it, we witnessed ancient memories of our people—wanderers who asked questions and died from the exact same illness spreading on my skin.".

Professor Ink listened with rapt attention, nodding solemnly.

"This aligns with Professor Kante's working thesis. Harmony's inability to synchronize with the Mizizi is rooted in a cultural taboo that your ancestors were explicitly forbidden to break. By breaking that social norm, you may have given us a hint on why we cannot form a node connection with the Mizizi.".

She paced across the laboratory deck, looking at each of the cadets in turn, her analytical mind whirring to connect the pieces.

"And this entity deliberately selected individuals from our camp. It stopped for Zephyr, which of course we know she is.. special. But it also stopped for Pip and Bramble you say, why?".

Ink turned toward Britt.

"Do you recognize which clans are represented here?".

Britt closed her eyes. In the quiet darkness behind his eyelids, the memory unlocked by the tortoise surfaced with crystal clarity—faces from the Great Clan Exchange that she had never been able to recall before.

"I remember them now," Britt said, opening his eyes and looking straight at Saffron and Iggy.

"There was an Earthkin woman who looked just like Iggy... and a pale, quiet scholar who carried the exact high-browed features of Saffron.".

Professor Ink's eyes widened in realization, "Saffron was with Pip and Bramble, yes? Rill please go find Saffron and bring her here immediately".

Chapter 13: The Sixth Clan

CHAPTER 13: THE SIXTH CLAN.

Rill returned from the upper decks leading Saffron by the hand. The pale Renali scholar's eyes were wide with apprehension, clutching her sketching pad against her chest as if the bustling laboratory were full of hungry predators.

Professor Ink stepped forward, softening her posture.

"Saffron... can you tell us where your people originate?".

Ignatius nudged Iggy with an elbow.

"Hey, Iggy—this is your specialty. Help her out.".

Iggy took a deliberate step backward, pulling his collar up.

"No. My specialty is the exact opposite of this.".

Professor Ink knelt slightly before Saffron, speaking with gentle urgency.

"It is vital to our expedition that we understand your origin. Are you from the central plains of Harmony?".

Saffron shook her head slowly, keeping her lips pressed tight.

"She doesn't speak," Aggie offered quietly from the examination table.

"She draws.".

"Do you have your sketchbook?"

Ink asked gently.

"Could you draw your home for us?".

Saffron hesitated, looking around at the circle of cadets. Seeing Aggie and Britt nod encouragingly, she pulled a piece of charcoal from her pocket and set her pad on the counter. With swift, elegant strokes, Saffron sketched a breathtaking landmass: an enormous, jagged mountain island floating entirely suspended in mid-air above the sea, completely disconnected from the earth below.

The room went completely silent as everyone stared at the impossible floating island.

Watching Saffron's sketch unlocked something deep within Iggy. Reaching onto the workbench, the little dirt-kin creature grabbed a quill, pulled a scrap of parchment toward him with a map of Vumbua, and without a single word, drew a heavy arrow plunging straight down through dark water to the absolute bedrock floor of the deep ocean.

Professor Ink studied both sketches, counting the clans on her fingers with rising awe.

"The Spirit Tortoise has deliberately assembled six distinct clan lineages aboard this vessel," Professor Ink declared softly.

"Zephyr representing the Storm-Callers; Ignatius from the Ash-Blood flame; Iggy from this place below the waves; Britt and Aggie from the Mizizi roots; Saffron from what appear to be floating islands; and Rill representing the ancient Wadi water.".

She looked up at the cadets, her determination absolute.

"I do not yet know what awaits us in the deep forest, but this creature is operating under an ancient, deliberate design. And that is more than reason enough to follow it.".

Britt stood up from the stool, rolling her shoulders.

"I'll help Lomi take the first watch on the bridge to keep our eyes locked on its path.".

"Let's move," Professor Ink commanded.

Chapter 14: The Old Growth

CHAPTER 14: THE OLD GROWTH.

For two days, the walker Elijah galloped southward across the plains, maintaining a strict watch rotation at the bridge helm so that no cadet ever broke visual contact with Mwaza-Kasa's wake in the grass.

On the third morning, the savanna gave way to towering ancient timbers. The petrified canopy thickened into an impenetrable labyrinth of colossal moss-draped trunks, forcing Elijah to grind to a halt at the edge of the forbidden old growth. The expedition disembarked onto the damp loam, continuing on foot into territory that Mizizi elders had explicitly forbidden their youth from ever entering.

At the center of a wide, mist-shrouded clearing stood the largest living organism any of them had ever witnessed—a colossal, ancient primordial tree whose petrified roots coiled across the clearing like sleeping dragons.

Encircling the base of the massive trunk was a thirty-foot ring of dense, glowing neon-green fungus—the exact lethal organism Rill had identified from the canyon caves, and that Britt had stumbled across in her explorations.

Rill gasped in pure horror, stumbling back.

"They're cultivating it..."

Rill breathed in terrified disbelief.

"How is that even possible?!".

Mwaza-Kasa crawled steadily to the edge of the clearing, turned back to meet the gaze of each member of the party, and then waddled straight into the ring of lethal fungus. Reaching the ancient bark, the giant Spirit Tortoise pressed its front limb against the wood—and collapsed motionless to the earth.

Ignatius cried out in alarm, jumping forward.

"Don't touch that! Did the turtle just die?!".

Chapter 14: Eight Vials

CHAPTER 14: EIGHT VIALS.

Trying to learn more about her surroundings, Aggie walked to an adjacent sentinel tree on the edge of the clearing, placing her palms against its bark to commune with the roots. But the wood remained cold, silent, and petrified - there was no life inside the bark of the trees surrounding the grove, they were solid stone.

Rill unslung her satchel, stepping up to the perimeter.

"I have eight vials of stabilizing antidote," Rill announced firmly.

"It won't cure us permanently, but it gives us time. If we are going to touch that tree and uncover what happened here... we take the draught together.".

Iggy didn't wait to be invited.

Grabbing a vial and knocking it back, he pulled his heavy trench coat tight around his dirt-kin frame, then marched straight through the thirty-foot perimeter of glowing fungal spores. The toxic dust swirled around him as he reached the fallen tortoise, kneeling beside its shell, he touched the trunk and also fell asleep.

Ignatius blinked, looking around the clearing in confusion.

"Where'd Iggy go? Wait—did he just fall asleep immediately?".

Before anyone could answer, Zephyr snatched a vial of her own, vaulted over the roots, and charged headlong through the fungal mist to slap her palm flat against the petrified trunk, dropping into the moss beside Iggy a heartbeat later.

Ignatius threw his hands in the air, embers flaring wildly at his cuffs.

"Fuck, I better go," he groaned.

"Iggy is going to be so pissed that Zephyr followed him in there!".

Britt stepped forward, rolling her shoulders and staring down at the vials in Rill's hands. Her dreadlocks of living root shifted with quiet resolve.

"I'm going too," she said firmly.

"I already carry the infection anyway, so I might as well.".

Professor Ink adjusted her brass spectacles, stepping forward to study the glowing veins pulsing beneath the bark.

"I believe one representative from each of the clans should take a vial," the professor observed.

"And perhaps two others—those who feel the deepest resonance with the network—should join them.".

Rill nodded in quiet agreement.

"Wherever this leads, we need to go together. It shouldn't be me—I don't possess a connection to the Mizizi network. But two non-clansmen who are willing to take the risk could step forward.".

Safrron who was looking at Professor Ink shaking her head near-panic, caught the attention of Pip, "Saffron, why are you shaking your head?"

Pip demanded, bouncing on her heels.

"Are you a clan member? Saffron? Saffron! That's SO COOL WHY DIDN'T YOU TELL US?!".

"Pip, let her be," Bramble rumbled softly, extending a vine to gently tug the excitable pixie back.

Meeting the calm, confident and supportive gaze of Bramble, Saffrons panic was replaced with a hint of shame. then determination. She nodded before reaching to grab a vial of her own from Rill and stepped up to lay her slender fingers against the living wood, collapsing gently into the moss.

Next, Lomi pushed his flat cap back, stepping out from the shadow of the stone terrace.

"I'll take one, Rill" he said simply, "if you're willing.".

"Makes sense to me, Lomi," Rill replied, extending a vial toward him.

Lomi took the glass cylinder, popped the stopper, and downed the bitter draught in a single gulp. He grimaced then chased the taste a drag of Grease he pulled from a flask in his pocket, before walking calmly to the tree and placing his bare hand against the bark. His knees folded beneath him as the ancient resonance pulled him under.

That left only a single open place.

Lucky and Pip stepped forward at the exact same instant, stopping inches apart and glaring at each other.

Lucky crossed his arms, his confident smile wavering slightly as he eyed the ominous, pulsing spores.

"Look... it just kind of feels like if one of us is going to get through this without a scratch, it's probably going to be me.".

Pip planted her tiny boots into the moss and jabbed a fierce finger at her own chest.

"No, dude! They like me way more than you!".

Lucky hesitated, looking between the colossal petrified tree and the stubborn pixie. Muttering under his breath, "Maybe I shouldnt bring my so -called luck into this."

he took a step back, and gave Pip a shrug, sweeping an arm toward the oak he said out loud, " You know what? You're right. Be my guest.".

Pip puffed her chest in triumph—and then froze.

Her giant eyes went wide with sudden, horrified realization.

"Oh shit..."

she squeaked, her voice climbing an octave.

"Did I just volunteer myself?!".

She whipped around toward Rill, waving both hands in desperate agitation.

"Quick before a change my mind. Give me! Give me!".

Snatching the final vial, Pip downed the liquid, closed her eyes, and sprinted full speed through the glowing spore cloud, and slammed her forehead with a resounding thwack straight into the petrified trunk—knocking herself out cold as she tumbled into a heap on the moss.

Chapter 15: The Ancestral Vision

CHAPTER 15: THE ANCESTRAL VISION.

As each of the clan membners and their firends touched petrified wood, the clearing at Center Grove dissolved. One by one - they entered the same series of visions, though they would not know this until they came out the other side.

The air did not merely blur—it fractured. Space unfolded like ancient parchment, and the world of mud, canvas tents, and iron machinery was torn away in a blinding rush of luminous teal Aether.

It was not a dream, nor was it a simple illusion cast upon the mind. It felt like stepping into the memory of a stranger—seeing through eyes that had turned to dust a thousand years before, feeling the secondhand warmth of fires long extinguished, hearing the voices of a forgotten age. The vision belonged to Mwaza-Kasa, stored within the quiet, immortal shell of the Spirit Tortoise. It did not invite them in as participants. It allowed them to witness as the tortoise had always witnessed—patient, ancient, observant, and utterly without judgement.

An each in their own mind, they watched as outside observers peering into secondhand memory. They saw the living reality of people, places, and sparks as they unfolded across time.

ACT I: THE FIRST UNION.

The world was vast, wild, and fragmented into silence. On a jet-black volcanic sand beach under a heavy blanket of tropical sea mist, two primitive peoples lived in absolute isolation, separated by hostile terrain.

On the left, shivering beneath simple structures build under the broad, dripping leaves of a dense, cold rainforest, huddled the early root-dwellers—turtle-fungus humanoids with dark scaled skin, clutching woven ivy shawls around their lumpy shells, living in damp misery without the warmth of fire. On the right, silhouetted against roaring lava vents and glowing magma crags, huddled the smoldering warriors of the volcanic peaks—their dark obsidian skin dusted with soot, literal crowns of orange flame burning from their scalps, possessing raw elemental heat but devoid of architecture, shifting unfomrtably as they tried to sleep no the bare volcanic rock.

Between them lay the neutral ground of wet black sand, where the turquoise tide crashed indifferently.

From the forest edge stepped a tall, regal turtle-kin elder, leaning on a staff of petrified ironbark. From the volcanic crags stepped a towering warrior chieftain in beaten bronze scale armor, embers smoldering in his yellow-orange eyes.

They possessed no shared language. Neither knew a single word the other spoke.

Standing on the wet black sand, knowing no words, each leader chose to draw the living spark of their people into the earth.

The smoldering warrior knelt, holding a glowing shard of volcanic glass, and seared a smooth, stepped sun-spire fire arc into the jet-black sand. The root-kin elder stepped forward, raised his petrified staff, and struck it straight through the center of the arc, carving a deep, vertical root-ladder spine.

A connection was born. The first union between clans.

The meeting unleashed an explosive era of cultural and physical creation. The ancient world did not build cold, mechanical engines or combust fossil fuels; their technology was an organic, elemental marvel powered by their living sparks.

Root woodcraft and volcanic thermal engineering combined. Smiths and wood-weavers worked side by side, fitting glowing bronze heat conduits through living ironbark timber frames, creating the comfortable, climate-controlled homes for the clans. Above every doorway, the combined two-stroke petroglyph mandala was deeply chiseled into the lintel. Inside the warm, glowing rooms, the amber light of core-fire lamps cast shadow puppets across polished timber walls, where families of both clans sat together, laughing in the initial joy of mutual discovery.

And one after another, as the joined clans discovered next. The Deep, the Storm, the Air, and the Water, connections were formed, and an empire began to grow.

ACT II: THE SYNERGISTIC MESH OF SPARKS. The web expanded, and with every clan that joined the union, the elemental sparks did not merely coexist—they interlocked, multiplying one another's capabilities and enabling each civilization to achieve what had once been physically impossible.

In the dark ocean caverns where waves crashed against towering basalt cliffs, the subterranean clay-kin huddled on cold ledges. Short, rounded humanoids of packed brown clay and smooth stone, wearing dark green seaweed robes pinned with polished silver pauldrons, they were master masons who longed to build cities in the ocean depths, but could never survive the freezing cold or the crushing pressure of the abyss.

The alliance provided the key. The sky-dwellers' mastery over atmospheric air currents and barometric pressure allowed the clay-kin to regulate the pressure inside deep-sea habitats, creating breathable, climate-controlled stone domes beneath the waves. Combined with flexible root-wood scaffolding and volcanic thermal bronze conduits, the clay-kin constructed colossal, luminous cities inside subterranean ocean caves. Bioluminescent teal root-lamps lit stone walkways, while heated water channels flowed past carved basalt colonnades.

And at the center of the entire empire stood the root-kin archivists. The living petrified oak forests served as the grand archive of the world. Archivist scholars meticulously encoded and preserved the complex resonance formulas in the living tree bark, teaching every clan how to weave their elemental sparks together into harmonious, living circuits.

In the sandstone canyons, the canyon-dwellers built terraced cliffside gardens fed by volcanic thermal warmth, subterranean mineral soil, and root-kin botanical design. High above in the heavens, the sky-dwellers transformed their frozen floating sky-isles into glorious terraced step-ziggurats and crystal spires suspended on heavy copper cables, their giant biological dragonflies pulling elegant wooden sky-chariots between landing pads.

Atop the central sky-altar, a graceful sky-scholar in flowing purple silk placed a glowing turquoise crystal sphere into the completed mandala plate.

"The circle is woven!" she cried as golden light flared across the ziggurat.

"One Mandala!" the elders answered in unison. "One Empire!".

ACT III: THE GOLDEN APEX & THE COMFORTABLE ROT. For a golden age, there was unmatched, effortless prosperity.

The Grand Forum of the Sun-Spire stood as the pinnacle of achievement: colossal white marble plazas framed by living petrified oak towers that reached toward the clouds. Iridescent biological dragonflies glided through azure skies in graceful arcs. The central petroglyph mandala on the imperial spire glowed with unbroken, radiant teal light.

From the forum balcony, the Empress of the Golden Age addressed the multitudes: "People of the Five Domains! As long as our connection endures, this golden age will never end!".

And that was the lie that doomed them.

Generations passed in effortless luxury. Surrounded by boundless abundance, society stopped challenging itself. Because survival required zero effort, genuine curiosity and discovery ground to a complete halt.

Citizens reclined lazily on silk couches in the grand plazas, eating fruit and ignoring hairline fractures in the conduits. Clan boundaries blurred into a comfortable, homogenized mediocrity. At council tables, leaders waved away new ventures with a complacent shrug: "So much effort to do new things... why bother? We already have everything we could ever need right here.".

In the high Imperial Observatory, a colossal copper-and-stone floor mosaic world map of Vumbua spanned the chamber. A central astrolabe cast shifting seasonal shadows across the floor—spring blossom giving way to summer sun, autumn leaves falling across the stone, winter frost coating the arched windows.

Generations walked indifferently over the map, never once looking out toward the uncharted horizons.

An aging architect in brass spectacles looked down at the dust gathering on the map's outer edges.

"My Empress..." the architect murmured, shaking his head. "The surveyors turned back at the borders. Not because they feared the Dark Undone... but because they saw exploration as pointless effort. They simply said we have enough right here.".

The Empress looked at her fading silk robes, her voice hollow with grief. "We lied to ourselves. Resting on our successes was our decay.".

ACT IV: THE BREAKDOWN & THE REGRESSION OF WAR. Because the people refused to grow or strive, the living elemental sparks began to suffocate.

The physical infrastructure of the empire began to fracture. In the deep sea habitats, the atmospheric pressure seals maintained by sky-air currents failed, and crushing ocean water violently shattered the clay-kin glass domes. In the skies, giant biological dragonflies—overloaded with luxury cargo and heavy passenger cabins—strained and flipped in mid-air, plunging into the cloud sea. Atop the basalt step-pyramids, unmaintained cooling channels ran dry, and lightning conductors exploded under storm strikes, showering the streets in fire and masonry.

The time of abundance was over.

Panic, famine, and accusation spread like wildfire. A toxic belief took root across the five domains: War is the answer. War will force an evolution. War will reignite the dying sparks! So the clans went to war.

All five domains clashed across their once-glorious cities in a catastrophic grand melee. But the tragedy deepened with every battle: the most advanced weapons were compound multi-spark constructs—magma cannons that required volcanic fire channeled through canyon cooling conduits; lightning ballistas that required tempest voltage focused through barometric air barrels; hydraulic pressure rams that required subterranean masonry powered by root tension.

As cross-clan harmony shattered and the individual sparks lost power, every compound weapon failed completely. Magma cannons sputtered into cold slag.

Lightning-arc ballistas cracked and shorted out. Hydraulic rams seized.

The war tragically regressed into crude, primitive medieval butchery. Soldiers who had once commanded living elemental physics were forced to slaughter one another with crude iron swords, wooden spears, and heavy siege catapults.

Yet no matter how much blood was spilled, the sparks did not return. The sparks had continued to decay, suffocating and growing dimmer with every passing generation that clung to past glories. Without them, absolute extinction loomed.

ACT V: THE SPARK-SOUL TRUTH & THE GOLDILOCKS CONDUIT. While the surface world tore itself apart, the cross-clan council of scholars met in a secret subterranean stone vault beneath the ancient roots.

The scholars gathered in the dim candlelight were dying, their physical frames bearing the horrifying marks of their failing sparks. Across the stone table, a volcanic ember scholar strained with all his might just to coax a faint, pathetic spark from his hair. Beside him, a root-kin archivist clutched his temples in agonizing pain, suffering catatonic seizures whenever he attempted to recall memories from five years past. A canyon scholar stared in hollow despair at a cracked, bone-dry clay water vessel, while a sky-dweller struggled simply to stir a breath of air in the stifling chamber.

A root-kin spore-scholar unrolled a glowing parchment scroll depicting living roots intertwined with human heart-sparks, his voice trembling with terrible certainty.

"Each civilization's elemental spark is not a tool," the scholar revealed. "It is an integral part of our soul. As the decay intensified, it began consuming the sparks. When the spark truly dies... it will take our souls with it. We will not survive.".

Silence fell over the vault.

The spore-scholar lifted a small dual-chambered glass conduit filled with a tiny, trickling stream of glowing teal sand.

"The war purged our requirement to sustain a large population," the scholar explained softly. "We must find a way to live off the very little we have left, without upsetting the delicate balance. We do not have enough will left to create a massive new connection that could save us, and if we grow with what we have the decayed network will collapse, and it will take us with it. But if we establish The Exchange—a tiny, controlled conduit that trades just enough connection between our peoples—it will move just enough resonance to keep our soul-sparks alive in isolation, until a new generation learns how to truly grow.".

ACT VI: THE WANTILA ROOT & THE MEMORY PURGE. The decision was sealed in sorrow.

At the perimeter of the ancient forest, a multi-clan coalition gathered to fell the great petrified timber canopy. Subterranean masons swung heavy iron axes, volcanic warriors scorched trunks with forge torches, canyon dwellers pulled two-man crosscut saws, and sky dwellers hauled heavy ropes. Colossal petrified trunks crashed into the dust, leaving a desolate wasteland of stumps.

An ember-kin scholar placed a comforting hand on the shoulder of a weeping root-kin archivist.

"You know these memories and this bark must die," the ember scholar said gently.

"If they remain, your children will remember what was lost. They will seek it out before they are ready—and collapse the fragile circuit, bringing doom upon us all.".

"We must at least keep the oldest grove," the root archivist wept, "or our spark will die anyway.".

To ensure no curious wanderer ever stumbled upon the remaining anchor, a canyon scholar planted a glowing, toxic-green root around the base of the central petrified oak in Center Grove: the Wantila root.

"We who dwell in the canyons will plant this Wantila root," the canyon scholar whispered somberly. "It will splatter invisibly upon any who draw near, poisoning them slowly and painlessly. I will teach your elders how to tend it...

but I will never teach you how to cure it. That knowledge must stay with the Wadi to protect us all.".

"We will teach our youth to treat this grove as a taboo of death," the root archivist answered, lowering his head. "If they will not listen, it is better that one curious wanderer die than our entire people perish. May the future forgive what we have unleashed upon them.".

Deep beneath the surface, in the subterranean root conduits, root-kin archivists pressed glowing cyan mycelium strands against their temples. A massive wave of dark, memory-purging psychic energy pulsed through the root network, systematically wiping every memory of the grand empire, the golden age, and the other clans from the minds of the populace.

In the vision's final, breathtaking instant, five hands—turtle-kin, ember-kin, clay-kin, tempest-kin, and sky-kin—placed their clan rings onto the central stone pact tablet.

The central spire flame died. The subterranean vault shattered in a deafening acoustic rupture, tearing space into a swirling vortex of high-frequency teal energy.

And as the portal spun, the ancient Spirit Tortoise itself turned its massive head within the river of memory. Its glowing golden-teal eyes met the gazes of the eleven travelers directly, conveying the profound truth across the millennia: it had carried and guarded these forbidden memories through the long dark, keeping the truth alive in its living shell until a generation arrived that was ready to learn, connect, and grow again.

Chapter 16: Momentum Is Life

CHAPTER 16: MOMENTUM IS LIFE.

Consciousness snapped back into their bodies like a bowstring released.

The damp forest floor. The twilight shadows of Center Grove. The ancient petrified oak, silent and colossal against the darkening sky.

First to react, Pip rolled out of the thirty-foot ring of glowing fungus, shaking her head vigorously like a wet dog.

"Whoa! That one was way cooler!"

Pip shouted, sitting up in the moss with an undignified grin.

"I am definitely getting out of this toxic stuff now, though!".

Scrambling to her feet on the safe turf, Pip turned around and stopped dead in her tracks.

In the center of the clearing, Mwaza-Kasa was rising.

The colossal Spirit Tortoise pushed itself up from the damp soil, straightening its massive, pillar-like legs. As the ancient beast lifted its head into the twilight air, the surface of its immense carapace ignited with soft, radiant energy.

Across the dark keratin scutes, ancient growth ridges and glowing veins of bioluminescent teal lichen formed a living, organic topographic map of the clan lands. Embedded directly into the natural shell plates, small pinpricks of runic light pulsed with elemental resonance, marking the forgotten strongholds of the lost world: the suspended sky-ziggurats of the Renali high above the cloud layer; the jagged mountain step-pyramids of the Fulgur; the terraced sandstone canyons of the Wadi; the fiery volcanic crags of the Ash-Blood; and, stretching across the deep oceanic basin, several distinct, glowing coordinates that marked the submerged cavern cities of the Trench-Kin.

Iggy did not scramble away., he stood frozen at the base of the petrified tree, his trembling hands hovering in the air as if they belonged to a stranger. Water sloshed heavily against the curved glass of his oversized goggles as he stared at the glowing oceanic runes on the shell.

As the rest of the group rose to their feet to gather around the map that Harmony could only dream of discovering.

"My whole life is a lie..."

Iggy whispered, his voice cracking with profound shock.

He dropped to his knees beside the ancient tortoise. For centuries, the deepest law of the Earthkin had been silence, secrecy, and absolute isolation from the surface world. But as the memory of the dying empire burned in his mind, Iggy's jaw hardened. In an open, deliberate act of rebellion against centuries of clan tradition, Iggy raised a shaking, clay-stained finger and jabbed it firmly onto the glowing ocean coordinates on the shell.

He looked up, meeting the eyes of the entire squad.

"Right here," Iggy declared fiercely, his voice ringing across the quiet clearing.

"This is where my people are. In the deep ocean trenches. That's where you'll find the Trench-Kin.".

Beside him, Saffron knelt on the damp moss. Her slender, pale fingers traced slow, deliberate circles over the glowing cluster of runes marking her sky-ziggurat, committing the forgotten coordinates to memory.

Iggy looked across the circle of cadets, his gaze resolute.

"Isolation was never the answer.".

Lomi leaned back against the mossy stone terrace, pushing his flat cap back and exhaling a long, ragged breath. He looked across the clearing at the stunned squad.

"Yeah. I just left Harmony for the first time today, so this is a lot to take in.".

Professor Ink stepped back from the tree, the brass-bound resonant crystal device in her hand suddenly erupting into a high, chiming hum as teal and emerald light pulsed across its dials.

"You've done it!"

she gasped, her eyes wide behind her spectacles.

"It's connected! What happened?".

The communication stone in Lomi's pocket crackled to life, and Professor Kante's voice crackled through the crystal speaker in breathless excitement.

"Professor Ink—there is a massive spike in the resonance! We're over the threshold!".

Beneath their boots, the forest floor shuddered.

Vibrant green shoots burst through the petrified soil—not uniformly, but surging outward in living waves from where the network had been touched most newly. Tiny petrified trees and golden moss erupted in thick clusters around Pip's still-breathing form, while fresh ivy sprouted directly between Lomi's heavy boots.

Uhmm what's happening? shrieked Pip as the growth was particularly heave around her and Lomi.

Rill stared at the racing growth in awe.

"I think it just downloaded Harmony."

Rill quickly filled in Professor Ink on what she had seen in the vision, with the whol egroup agreeing that is what they had seen too.

"Knowledge!"

Professor Ink exclaimed, scribbling frantically into her field journal with one hand while clutching the singing device with the other.

"Your spark is knowledge! That's all it took—storing information here in the living network, exactly like we stored records of the clans in Harmony Prime! That's literally Harmony's information growing right now!".

Ignatius crossed his arms, embers flickering at his cuffs as he stepped toward the trunk.

"I mean, I think it's less about knowledge and more about cooperation, right?".

"Cooperation yes, that forms the connection, but I think it's more specifc!"

Professor Ink insisted, gesturing with her quill.

"They called them sparks, and the specific spark of the Mizizi was storing memory!".

"Yeah," Ignatius conceded with a thoughtful nod.

"Yeah, I guess so.".

"And now it downloaded that information through people walking the network!"

Professor Ink beamed.

"For what I believe is the first time from anyone outside the Mizizi in centuries!".

Pip, overcoming her initial fear of the growth, scrambled to her feet and went skipping through the clearing, tiny yellow flowers and wild ivy shoots blooming under her heels with every step she took. She skidded to a halt and looked down at her boots, then beamed at the towering plant-kin.

"Brambies, Brambies! I'm like you! I'm making the plants grow, Bramble!".

Are we at all concerned that the first knowledge stored about Harmony will be from Pip and Lomi? Val asked Lucky with a touch of concern.

"Ehh I'm sure it will be fine.."

Lucky replied while they both watched the halfling skip around the clearing.

In the ancient tongue they were called Sparks; in the modern terminology of the Academy they were classified as Nodes. But the underlying cosmic truth was identical: each civilization had adapted to the harshest, most extreme frontiers of the world—the crushing ocean depths, the volcanic island calderas, the lightning-swept mountain peaks, the sandstone canyon aqueducts, the floating sky-ziggurats, and the living root-forests.

In isolation, each spark was finite, vulnerable to stagnation, and destined to suffocate under its own comfort. But when woven into a unified circuit, the energy was not merely additive—it was exponential, multiplying the vitality of the world beyond the reach of decay.

Lomi adjusted his flat cap, studying the glowing runic coordinates shining across Mwaza-Kasa's shell.

"Harmony kept expecting massive power surges with every node they logged," Lomi murmured, his mechanical intuition piercing the heart of the mystery.

"But until all six clans are found and reconnected, the circuit is choked. We've only been drawing a fractional trickle through the dust. That's why the arena spires failed. That's why the storm tore through the shields.".

"And when they are connected?"

Ignatius asked, embers glowing warmly in his eyes as he looked toward the dark canopy above.

"What happens when every clan on the map is found?".

"Then we keep going," Lomi said simply, a broad, easy smile spreading across his soot-smudged face.

"We build faster rigs. We chart uncharted oceans. And if there is no land left on this continent, we build vessels that can sail through the stars to find other worlds.".

"Exploration isn't a trade or an academy degree," Aggie whispered, resting her palm gently against the rough, warm keratin of the tortoise's front leg.

"It's the only thing keeping the heart of this world beating.".

Rill stepped to the center of the mossy stone stairs, looking across the sacred clearing at the assembled eleven companions.

"If we connect them all," Rill said softly, her blue hair stirring in the rising evening wind, "then we stabilize the resonance decay. The sickness halts. The barriers fall.

And the clans can finally come home."

She paused, meeting their eyes one by one in the twilight glow.

"I get it now, Momentum is life.".
